items.stem: Which is the best thermal conductor?
items.answer: Copper
items.markingKey: Metals are good conductors; copper is one of the best.

items.stem: Explain why metals conduct thermal energy much better than non-metals.
items.answer: In both, vibrating particles pass energy to neighbours, but metals also have free electrons that move quickly through the metal and collide with distant particles, transferring energy much faster.
items.markingKey: lattice vibrations in both [1]; free electrons in metals [1]; move rapidly, transfer energy further [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon in the same drawer, although both are at the same temperature.
items.answer: The metal conducts thermal energy away from your hand much faster, so your skin cools more quickly.
items.markingKey: same temperature [1]; metal conducts energy from hand faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe heats one end of four rods of equal size, each with a ball of wax stuck to the far end with a dab of wax. Times for the wax to melt and the ball to fall: iron 109 s, brass 75 s, aluminium 38 s, steel 140 s. (a) Rank the rods from best to worst conductor. (b) State two variables that must be controlled. (c) Explain why the best conductor transfers energy fastest.
items.answer: (a) aluminium, brass, iron, steel (b) same length and thickness of rods; same heating (same flame position/temperature); same amount of wax (c) aluminium is a metal with many free electrons moving quickly to transfer energy.
items.markingKey: (a) correct order (shortest time = best) [1] (b) two control variables [2] (c) free electrons [1] [4]

items.stem: Mei heats one end of four rods of equal size, each with a ball of wax stuck to the far end with a dab of wax. items.stem: A cook in Karachi chooses a pan with a copper base, steel sides and a plastic handle. (a) Explain why the base of the pan is made of copper. (b) Explain why a thin layer of air under a pan on an uneven hob slows heating.
items.answer: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor (free electrons), so energy reaches the food quickly. (b) Air is a poor conductor, so less energy is conducted to the pan.
items.markingKey: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor (free electrons) [1]; so energy reaches the food quickly [1] [2] (b) Air is a poor conductor [1]; so less energy is conducted to the pan [1] [2]

options: They have free (delocalised) electrons that carry energy quickly
items.answer: They have free (delocalised) electrons that carry energy quickly

items.stem: Explain why saucepans are made of metal but have plastic or wooden handles.
items.answer: Metal conducts thermal energy quickly from the cooker to the food; the handle is an insulator so it stays cool enough to hold.
items.markingKey: metal pan conducts to food [1]; insulating handle [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why liquids and gases are poor conductors.
items.answer: Their particles are further apart (especially in gases), so vibrations are passed on less effectively, and there are no free electrons.
items.markingKey: particles far apart [1]; no free electrons [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor (free electrons), so energy reaches the food quickly. (b) Vibrating ions pass energy to neighbours and free electrons move through the metal, colliding with ions.
items.markingKey: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor (free electrons) [1]; so energy reaches the food quickly [1] [2] (b) Vibrating ions pass energy to neighbours and free electrons move through the metal [1]; colliding with ions [1] [2]

items.stem: Convection can occur in …
items.answer: liquids and gases
items.markingKey: Convection needs a fluid that can flow.

items.stem: Explain how a convection current forms in a room heated by a radiator.
items.answer: Air next to the radiator is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air moves in to replace it; the warm air cools near the ceiling and far wall and sinks, forming a circulating current.
items.markingKey: air heated and expands [1]; less dense rises [1]; cooler air sinks/replaces → circulation [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why sea breezes blow from the sea towards the land during a sunny day.
items.answer: The land heats up faster than the sea; air above the land is warmed and rises; cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it.
items.markingKey: land warms faster [1]; warm air rises over land [1]; cool air from sea replaces it [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara is designing the position of one electric heater and one air-conditioning unit in an office. Suggest the best position and explain using ideas about density and convection.
items.answer: Heater low down (near the floor): warmed air expands, becomes less dense and rises, circulating around the room. Air-conditioner high up: cooled air is denser and sinks, spreading through the room.
items.markingKey: sensible position [1]; heated fluid expands/less dense rises or cooled fluid denser sinks [1]; applied to context [1] [3]

items.stem: An engineer in Auckland must decide where to put the cooling unit in a new drinks refrigerator for a shop. Suggest the best position and explain using ideas about density and convection.
items.answer: At the top: air cooled there becomes denser and sinks over the drinks; warmer air rises to the top to be cooled, giving a convection current.
items.markingKey: sensible position [1]; heated fluid expands/less dense rises or cooled fluid denser sinks [1]; applied to context [1] [3]

items.stem: A crystal of purple dye is placed at one side of the bottom of a beaker of water and the beaker is heated gently beneath the crystal. (a) Describe the path of the dye after it reaches the surface. (b) Predict what would happen if the beaker were heated at the top instead.
items.answer: (a) It spreads across the top, then sinks down the cooler side and returns along the bottom: a convection current. (b) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense); little convection, so the bottom stays cool.
items.markingKey: (a) It spreads across the top, then sinks down the cooler side and returns along the bottom [1]; a convection current [1] [2] (b) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense) [1]; little convection, so the bottom stays cool [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe an experiment to show convection currents in water.
items.answer: Drop a crystal of potassium permanganate into a beaker of water near one edge of the base; heat gently below the crystal; the purple colour rises above the heat, moves across the top and sinks at the other side.
items.markingKey: crystal at side of base [1]; heat below it [1]; describe circulating path [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why an air-conditioning unit is usually fitted high on a wall.
items.answer: The cool air it produces is denser and sinks, spreading through the room and setting up a convection current.
items.markingKey: cool air sinks [1]; circulation [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe and explain the convection in magma in the Earth’s mantle.
items.answer: Hot rock rises slowly and cooler rock sinks. Heated fluid expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks.
items.markingKey: heated fluid becomes less dense and rises [1]; cooler fluid sinks [1]; applied to the context [1] [3]

items.stem: Sipho is designing the position of the immersion heater in a domestic hot-water tank. Suggest the best position and explain using ideas about density and convection.
items.answer: Near the bottom: heated water rises to the top, where the hot tap is connected, and cold water sinks to be heated, so the whole tank warms.
items.markingKey: sensible position [1]; heated fluid expands/less dense rises or cooled fluid denser sinks [1]; applied to context [1] [3]

items.stem: A company in Mexico City asks for advice on the position of the heating element in a new design of electric kettle. Suggest the best position and explain using ideas about density and convection.
items.answer: At the bottom: water heated there expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser water sinks to be heated, so all the water is heated by convection.
items.markingKey: sensible position [1]; heated fluid expands/less dense rises or cooled fluid denser sinks [1]; applied to context [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the panels of a solar water heater are painted dull black.

items.answer: (a) dull (matt) black (b) it cooled the most (largest temperature drop in the same time). (c) same volume and starting temperature of water; same can size; same room conditions/no draughts; lids on.

items.stem: Explain how an increase in greenhouse gases leads to global warming.
items.answer: The Earth’s surface emits infrared; greenhouse gases absorb it and re-emit some back towards the Earth; more gases mean less energy escapes, so the Earth must warm until the outgoing rate again equals the incoming rate.
items.markingKey: surface emits infrared [1]; gases absorb/re-emit [1]; imbalance → temperature rise [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how each feature of a vacuum flask reduces thermal energy transfer.
items.answer: Vacuum: no conduction or convection; silvered walls: reduce radiation (poor emitter/good reflector); stopper: reduces convection and evaporation; insulating supports: reduce conduction.
items.markingKey: vacuum [1]; silvering [1]; stopper/supports [1] [3]

items.stem: Discuss how human activities may be changing the Earth’s energy balance and what the consequences could be.
items.answer: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation increase CO₂; more infrared is absorbed and re-emitted to the surface; less energy escapes so the Earth warms until a new balance; consequences: melting ice (less reflection, positive feedback), sea-level rise, extreme weather.

items.markingKey: sensible position [1]; heated fluid expands/less dense rises or cooled fluid denser sinks [1]; applied to context [1] [3]

items.stem: A crystal of purple dye is placed at one side of the bottom of a beaker of water and the beaker is heated gently beneath the crystal. (a) Explain why the dye rises above the flame. (b) Describe the path of the dye after it reaches the surface. (c) Predict what would happen if the beaker were heated at the top instead.
items.answer: (a) The water there is heated, expands, becomes less dense and rises. (b) It spreads across the top, then sinks down the cooler side and returns along the bottom: a convection current. (c) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense); little convection, so the bottom stays cool.
items.markingKey: (a) The water there is heated [1]; expands, becomes less dense and rises [1] [2] (b) It spreads across the top, then sinks down the cooler side and returns along the bottom [1]; a convection current [1] [2] (c) Hot water would stay at the top (less dense) [1]; little convection, so the bottom stays cool [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Thermal radiation can travel through … (b) Which surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation?
items.answer: (a) a vacuum (b) Dull black
items.markingKey: (a) It is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium. (b) Dull black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers.

items.stem: Explain why a person standing near a campfire feels warmer on the side facing the fire.
items.answer: Infrared radiation from the fire travels in straight lines and is absorbed by the side facing it; the other side is not in the path of the radiation.
items.markingKey: radiation travels in straight lines [1]; absorbed by facing side [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar fills three identical cans, painted dull (matt) black, dull white, shiny silver, with water at 80 °C and records the temperature after 20 minutes: dull (matt) black 56 °C, dull white 64 °C, shiny silver 72 °C. (a) State which surface is the best emitter. (b) Explain how the results show this. (c) State two variables that should be controlled.
items.answer: (a) dull (matt) black (b) it cooled the most (largest temperature drop in the same time). (c) same volume and starting temperature of water; same can size; same room conditions/no draughts; lids on.
items.markingKey: (a) correct surface [1] (b) largest drop in same time [1] (c) two controls [2] [4]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a house loses less energy if its walls and loft are insulated, using all three methods of transfer. (b) Explain why ice and snow melting in the Arctic can speed up global warming.
items.answer: (a) Insulating materials trap air, which reduces conduction; trapped air cannot circulate, reducing convection; foil backing reflects radiation. (b) Ice reflects most sunlight; when it melts, darker sea or land absorbs more radiation, warming the Earth further.
items.markingKey: (a) conduction [1]; convection [1]; radiation [1] [3] (b) ice reflects [1]; darker surface absorbs more [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why ice and snow melting in the Arctic can speed up global warming. (b) Explain how an increase in greenhouse gases leads to global warming.
items.answer: (a) Ice reflects most sunlight; when it melts, darker sea or land absorbs more radiation, warming the Earth further. (b) The Earth’s surface emits infrared; greenhouse gases absorb it and re-emit some back towards the Earth; more gases mean less energy escapes, so the Earth must warm until the outgoing rate again equals the incoming rate.
items.markingKey: (a) ice reflects [1]; darker surface absorbs more [1] [2] (b) surface emits infrared [1]; gases absorb/re-emit [1]; imbalance → temperature rise [1] [3]

items.stem: A saucepan has a copper base and a plastic handle. (a) Explain why the base of the pan is made of copper. (b) Explain why the handle is made of plastic. (c) Suggest why the lid reduces the time needed to heat the food.
items.answer: (a) Copper is an excellent conductor (free electrons), so energy reaches the food quickly. (b) Plastic is a poor conductor, so the handle stays cool. (c) Reduces energy loss by convection and evaporation.

items.stem: Mateo heats one end of four rods of equal size, each with a ball of wax stuck to the far end with a dab of wax. (c) Explain why the best conductor transfers energy fastest.
items.answer: (a) copper, aluminium, iron, glass (b) same length and thickness of rods; same heating (same flame position/temperature); same amount of wax (c) copper is a metal with many free electrons moving quickly to transfer energy.

items.stem: A saucepan has a copper base and a plastic handle. (a) Explain why the handle is made of plastic. (b) Describe how energy is conducted through the copper base. (c) Explain why a thin layer of air under a pan on an uneven hob slows heating.
items.answer: (a) Plastic is a poor conductor, so the handle stays cool. (b) Vibrating ions pass energy to neighbours and free electrons move through the metal, colliding with ions. (c) Air is a poor conductor, so less energy is conducted to the pan.
